questions.problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 3 & 7\end{aligned}],$ find the product of the eigenvalues of $A.$
questions.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2}=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the determinant of $A.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} & =det(A) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 3 & 7\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-4)\cdot 7-(-5)\cdot 3 \\  & =-28+15 \\  & =-13.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 4 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-8 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-5A-2 & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-5A-2) & ={A}^{-1}O \\ A-5I-2{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =-\frac{5}{2}I+\frac{1}{2}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-\frac{5}{2},$ $q=\frac{1}{2}$ and

$$
p+q=-\frac{5}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=-2.
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda),$ i.e., the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2}=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the sum of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the trace of $A.$ 

Therefore, 

$$
\lambda_1+\lambda_2 = \textrm{tr}(A)= 9+(-6)=3.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix such that $\textrm{tr}(A)=-4$ and $\textrm{det}(A)=-18.$ If $A^2 = xA + yI$ for constants $x$ and $y,$ then find the value of $x+y.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by 

$$
p(\lambda)=\lambda^2-\textrm{tr}(A)\lambda+\textrm{det}(A).
$$

Therefore, using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p(A) & =O \\ {A}^{2}-\text{tr}(A)A+\text{det}(A)I & =O \\ {A}^{2} & =\text{tr}(A)A-\text{det}(A)I \\ {A}^{2} & =-4A+18I.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x+y = -4+18 = 14.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-8-\lambda  & -9 \\ 6 & 7-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-8-\lambda )(7-\lambda )+54 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}+A-2I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by $A^{-1}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}+A-2I) & =O \\ A+I-2{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{1}{2}I\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\dfrac{1}{2},$ $q=\dfrac{1}{2},$ and 

$$
p+q=\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}=1.
$$

$\:\:x^{10}$
$x^2-1\:$ $\!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{x^{12} \, - \, x^{10} + 2x - 1 {\phantom{|}} }$
$x^{12}$ $-$ $x^{10}$
$2x$ $-$ $1$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & ={x}^{10}({x}^{2}-1)+(2x-1),\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x) = x^{10}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A) = q(A)p(A)+(2A-I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(2A-I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(2A-I) \\ & =2A-I \\ & =2[\begin{aligned}4 & -5 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -10 \\ 6 & -8\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -10 \\ 6 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

tutorials.name: The Characteristic Polynomial for 2x2 Matrices
tutorials.problem:
What conclusions can we make regarding the characteristic polynomial of the general $2\times 2$ matrix $A,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14131517/assets/8e26937ef1981804a548e92a4041bd8672cc75c7c5cc6efa0c0c2694c0736791.svg)

First, let's find the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \left|\begin{aligned}a-\lambda  & b \\ c & d-\lambda \end{aligned}\right| & =0 \\ (a-\lambda )(d-\lambda )-bc & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-(a+d)\lambda +(ad-bc) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the constant term is the determinant of the matrix: 

$$
\det(A) = ad-bc
$$

 

The coefficient of $\lambda$ is the sum of the diagonal entries of $A$ taken with a negative sign. The sum of the diagonal entries of a matrix $A$ is called the **trace** of $A,$ and we denote it as 

$$
\mathrm{tr}(A) = a+d.
$$

So, for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A$, the characteristic polynomial is

$$
p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 -\mathrm{tr}(A)\lambda + \det(A).
$$

**Note:** This result can be extended to the general case of $n \times n$ matrices. If $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix, then its characteristic polynomial takes the form

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(A-\lambda I) \\  & =(-1)^{n}{\lambda }^{n}+{c}_{n-1}{\lambda }^{n-1}+⋯+{c}_{1}\lambda +{c}_{0} \\  & =(-1)^{n}{\lambda }^{n}+{{(-1)^{n-1}\text{tr}(A)}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{n-1}}{\lambda }^{n-1}+⋯+{c}_{1}\lambda +{{det(A)}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{0}},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{n-1}=(-1)^{n-1}\text{tr}(A)\,\text{and}\,{c}_{0}=det(A).\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem to Quickly Evaluate a Matrix Polynomial
tutorials.problem:
If we want to evaluate a high-degree polynomial for a given matrix input, it can take a lot of time. For example, suppose we wanted to evaluate the polynomial

$$
f(x) = x^{10} - 5x^9 - 2x^8 + x + 2
$$

for the input ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14131517/assets/0f9bff826261a956305962b4ca945ed91012cc5042e6ffe92a4b5f1ce13d3237.svg) Computing the $10$th power of this matrix would be a lot of work!

Luckily, there is a way to speed up the process. The trick is to use Cayley-Hamilton theorem, which tells us that every matrix is a solution to its characteristic equation.

For the given matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14131517/assets/6514096b22aed47005e5ff59c47e3cec701aed5b120b0022b186f1bec941d953.svg) the characteristic polynomial is

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 3 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the Cayley-Hamilton theorem tells us that

$$
p(A) = A^2 - 5A - 2I = 0.
$$

Now, observe that the polynomial $f(x)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{10}-5{x}^{9}-2{x}^{8}+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}({x}^{2}-5x-2)+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}p(x)+x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then we have

$$
f(A) = A^8 p(A) + A + 2I,
$$

and because $p(A) = 0,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{8}\cdot 0+A+2I \\  & =0+A+2I \\  & =A+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the computation is much faster:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =A+2I \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Other times, it may not be so obvious how to group the terms of $f(x)$ to reveal $p(x).$ In the general case, it's best to divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division, and use the result

$$
f(x) = q(x) p(x) + r(x)
$$

where $q(x)$ is the quotient and $r(x)$ is the remainder. Let's see an example of this.

tutorials.title: Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem to Quickly Evaluate a Matrix Polynomial
tutorials.content:
If we want to evaluate a high-degree polynomial for a given matrix input, it can take a lot of time. For example, suppose we wanted to evaluate the polynomial

$$
f(x) = x^{10} - 5x^9 - 2x^8 + x + 2
$$

for the input ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14131517/assets/0f9bff826261a956305962b4ca945ed91012cc5042e6ffe92a4b5f1ce13d3237.svg) Computing the $10$th power of this matrix would be a lot of work!

Luckily, there is a way to speed up the process. The trick is to use Cayley-Hamilton theorem, which tells us that every matrix is a solution to its characteristic equation.

For the given matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14131517/assets/6514096b22aed47005e5ff59c47e3cec701aed5b120b0022b186f1bec941d953.svg) the characteristic polynomial is

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 3 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the Cayley-Hamilton theorem tells us that

$$
p(A) = A^2 - 5A - 2I = 0.
$$

Now, observe that the polynomial $f(x)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{10}-5{x}^{9}-2{x}^{8}+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}({x}^{2}-5x-2)+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}p(x)+x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then we have

$$
f(A) = A^8 p(A) + A + 2I,
$$

and because $p(A) = 0,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{8}\cdot 0+A+2I \\  & =0+A+2I \\  & =A+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the computation is much faster:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =A+2I \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Other times, it may not be so obvious how to group the terms of $f(x)$ to reveal $p(x).$ In the general case, it's best to divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division, and use the result

$$
f(x) = q(x) p(x) + r(x)
$$

where $q(x)$ is the quotient and $r(x)$ is the remainder. Let's see an example of this.
